sections.on_the_job: Come here in this order: Table 1 for the allowed percentage, Table 4 for the raceway, Table 5 for insulated conductors, and Table 8 when a voltage-drop check needs resistance. One pass through a real check: three or more conductors means 40 percent from Table 1; 1/2 in EMT allows 0.122 sq in at that percentage from Table 4; the conductors on the list — two 6 AWG THHN and one 10 AWG THHN — total 0.1225 sq in from Table 5, so the run goes up to 3/4 in EMT. Do not size conduit from a memorized count you heard on another job — raceway type, insulation type, and conductor count all change the answer.
sections.plain_explanation:
Chapter 9 is not a set of wiring rules for one kind of job. It is the data the rest of the book points back to:
• Table 1 — the percentage of a raceway conductors may occupy
• Table 2 — minimum radius of conduit bends
• Table 4 — raceway inside diameters and usable areas
• Table 5 and Table 5A — insulated and compact conductor dimensions and areas
• Table 8 — conductor properties and DC resistance, the voltage-drop input
• Table 9 — AC resistance and reactance, for finer voltage-drop work
• Tables 11(A) and 11(B) — how much power a Class 2 or Class 3 source may deliver
Behind the tables sit the informative annexes — Annex B on ampacity calculation under engineering supervision, Annex C's same-size fill tables, Annex D's worked load-calculation examples, Annex I's recommended torque values. Annex material explains and illustrates; it does not add mandatory requirements on its own.
sections.title: Chapter 9 — the table room
sections.why_it_exists: Every sizing answer in the trade is only as good as the table it came from. Chapter 9 keeps the numbers in one printed place, so a fill percentage, a raceway area and a resistance all trace to the same source instead of memory and habit. The annexes sit behind a fence for a reason: a worked example shows one way through a calculation, and treating an example as a rule is how a legal installation gets failed — or an illegal one gets built.
inspection_fails: Mixed-size pull sized from an Annex C count table, which only works when every conductor is the same size and type.
Fill figured from the EMT row of Table 4 for a PVC Schedule 40 run — the raceway installed is smaller inside than the raceway calculated.
Voltage-drop check run on a resistance remembered from another conductor size instead of the Table 8 row for the conductor in hand.
Annex example cited to the inspector as if it were a Code requirement.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats Annex C like a requirement table: 'Annex C says nine fit, so nine are legal.' Annex C is an informative shortcut built from Tables 1, 4 and 5 for same-size conductors only. It cannot bless a mixed-size pull, and no annex overrides the tables it was built from.

sections.figure_idea: Three circles showing the same raceway with one, two, and three-plus conductors shaded to 53, 31, and 40 percent.
sections.on_the_job: Count every conductor in the run, including the equipment grounding conductor, then pick the percentage for that count before you open Tables 4 and 5. The most common house and light-commercial case is three or more conductors, so 40 percent is the column you will use most — but never use it for a one- or two-conductor pull. Short stubs earn their own number: a 1/2 in EMT nipple has a 60 percent area of 0.182 sq in in Table 4, which at 0.0133 sq in for one 12 AWG THHN is 13 conductors by fill alone.
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 1 sets the share of a raceway's inside cross-section that conductors may take up:
• 1 conductor — 53 percent
• 2 conductors — 31 percent
• 3 or more conductors — 40 percent
• A nipple 24 in or less between enclosures — 60 percent, covered on the nipple page
The percentage is taken against the raceway's total inside area in Table 4, and the conductor areas come from Table 5. Those percentages already allow for the fact that conductors do not pack like water — two round conductors side by side waste more of the circle, which is why the two-conductor number is the lowest of the three.
sections.title: Table 1 — how much of a raceway you may fill
sections.why_it_exists: A raceway filled past its percentage cannot be pulled without a fight: conductors jam at the bends, insulation skins against the raceway wall, and a damaged jacket is a fault waiting for a damp day. The limits also leave the breathing room a bundled run needs. The odd dip at two conductors is geometry, not a typo — two circles side by side waste more of the pipe than one large conductor or a bundle of three or more.
inspection_fails: Two-conductor pull figured at 40 percent instead of 31 — the raceway is overfilled on the approved calculation itself.
Equipment ground left out of the conductor count, so a three-conductor run was figured as two — wrong percentage and the ground's own area missing.
The 60 percent nipple allowance applied to a full-length run between panels.
Percentage read off one raceway's Table 4 row and applied to another — an EMT answer used for a PVC run.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reaching for 40 percent every time because it is the familiar number. Two conductors get only 31 percent — a two-wire pull figured at 40 is overfilled before it starts. The reverse trap: 53 percent is not a bonus rate for three conductors. It belongs to a single conductor only.

sections.on_the_job: Worked check: a 1/2 in EMT nipple has a 60 percent area of 0.182 sq in in Table 4. At 0.0133 sq in for one 12 AWG THHN, that is 0.182 / 0.0133 = 13.68, so 13 conductors by fill alone. And Note 4 to Table 1 goes further than the 60%: the 310.15(C)(1) ampacity adjustment factors do NOT have to be applied to conductors in a nipple 24 in or shorter — the Code waives that check here expressly, so do not saddle the nipple with it.
sections.plain_explanation: A short raceway nipple — 24 inches or less between boxes, cabinets, or similar enclosures — may be filled to 60 percent instead of the Table 1 percentages. The extra room is allowed because a short, straight stub is far easier to pull and far less likely to jam than a long run. The allowance belongs to the nipple only; the long runs on either side of it still use 53, 31, or 40 percent as their conductor count requires.

sections.figure_idea: A 90-degree bend drawn with a dimension line running from the bend's center point to the conduit centerline, with two arcs shown — the tighter bender arc and the wider heat-bend arc — labelled with the two Table 2 columns.
sections.on_the_job:
A bender's shoe sets the radius for you: use the shoe made for the conduit type and size and the bend lands on the first column by construction. Heat-bent PVC is where crews get caught — form the sweep to at least the 'other bends' number, because a tight heat bend that kinks or flattens also fails the 'do not damage, do not effectively reduce the inside diameter' half of the bending sections.

Worked check: a 2 in PVC stub-up sweep formed at a 10 in centerline radius fails Table 2 by 2 in even if it looks smooth. Re-form it at 12 in or better before the concrete truck is called.
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 2 sets the smallest radius a field bend may have, measured to the centerline of the conduit — not to the inside face of the bend. It has two columns. Bends made on a one-shot or full-shoe bender use the first; all other bends use the second, and a PVC heat bend falls in the second column. The column is set by the bending method, not by a section number. The minimum centerline radii for the sizes Sharma bends most: • 1/2 in — 4 in one-shot / full-shoe, 4 in other bends
• 3/4 in — 4-1/2 in one-shot / full-shoe, 5 in other bends
• 1 in — 5-3/4 in one-shot / full-shoe, 6 in other bends
• 1-1/4 in — 7-1/4 in one-shot / full-shoe, 8 in other bends
• 1-1/2 in — 8-1/4 in one-shot / full-shoe, 10 in other bends
• 2 in — 9-1/2 in one-shot / full-shoe, 12 in other bends The table keeps climbing past 2 in — 2-1/2 in is 10-1/2 / 15 in and 4 in is 16 / 24 in — and runs to 6 in in the printed book. A factory sweep or a segmented bend laid out well above these numbers is fine; the table is a floor, not a target.

sections.plain_explanation:
Table 4 gives, for each raceway type and trade size, the inside diameter, the total inside area, and the usable area at each Table 1 percentage. Trade size is a name, not a measurement: 1/2 in EMT is actually 0.622 in inside and 0.304 sq in total, with 0.122 sq in usable at 40 percent. Raceway type matters as much as trade size — 1/2 in PVC Schedule 40 is a little smaller inside (0.285 sq in total, 0.114 at 40 percent), so an EMT answer does not carry over to PVC. Two more raceways are carried here so their answers are not borrowed from the wrong row. PVC Schedule 80, the thick-wall PVC used where conduit is subject to physical damage, runs smaller inside than Schedule 40 at every size (inside diameter in inches, total area in sq in, then the usable areas at 53, 31, and 40 percent): 1/2 in — 0.526, 0.217, 0.115, 0.067, 0.087; 3/4 in — 0.722, 0.409, 0.217, 0.127, 0.164; 1 in — 0.936, 0.688, 0.365, 0.213, 0.275; 1-1/4 in — 1.255, 1.237, 0.656, 0.383, 0.495; 1-1/2 in — 1.476, 1.711, 0.907, 0.530, 0.684; 2 in — 1.913, 2.874, 1.523, 0.891, 1.150. Flexible metal conduit (FMC) is its own row too — close to EMT at the small sizes, but never the same row: 1/2 in — 0.635, 0.317, 0.168, 0.098, 0.127; 3/4 in — 0.824, 0.533, 0.283, 0.165, 0.213; 1 in — 1.020, 0.817, 0.433, 0.253, 0.327; 1-1/4 in — 1.275, 1.277, 0.677, 0.396, 0.511; 1-1/2 in — 1.538, 1.858, 0.985, 0.576, 0.743; 2 in — 2.040, 3.269, 1.732, 1.013, 1.307. A fill that passes in Schedule 40 or EMT can fail in Schedule 80, so when the raceway changes, rerun the division with the new row.

The two raceways Sharma pulls most, carried here for the common sizes — total inside area first, then the usable area at 40 percent:
• 1/2 in EMT — 0.304 in² total, 0.122 in² at 40%
• 3/4 in EMT — 0.533 in² total, 0.213 in² at 40%

• 1-1/2 in EMT — 2.036 in² total, 0.814 in² at 40%
• 2 in EMT — 3.356 in² total, 1.342 in² at 40%
PVC Schedule 40 runs a little smaller inside than EMT at every trade size:
• 1/2 in PVC Schedule 40 — 0.285 in² total, 0.114 in² at 40%
• 3/4 in PVC Schedule 40 — 0.508 in² total, 0.203 in² at 40%

sections.on_the_job: Confirm the insulation type on the reel before you calculate. If the job switches from THHN to a thicker insulation type, redo the fill math with that type's Table 5 area instead of assuming the count still fits.
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 5 gives the approximate diameter and area of insulated conductors and fixture wires, by size and insulation type. Fill is figured on the insulated conductor you are actually pulling, insulation included — not on the bare metal. In the v1 data used throughout this chapter, 12 AWG THHN/THWN/THWN-2 is 0.0133 sq in, 10 AWG is 0.0211, 8 AWG is 0.0366, and 6 AWG is 0.0507. A different insulation type in the same AWG can have a different area, so the insulation column is part of the answer.

sections.title: Table 5 — how much room an insulated conductor takes
Table 5A — compact conductor dimensions and areas
sections.plain_explanation: Table 5A is Table 5's sibling for compact-stranded conductors. In a compact conductor the strands are compressed during manufacture, so the finished conductor is rounder and smaller across than a standard concentric-stranded conductor of the same AWG — a stranding common in larger aluminum feeder conductors. Fill is figured on the conductor actually in the raceway: compact conductors take their diameter and area from Table 5A, standard conductors from Table 5. Figuring a compact conductor from Table 5 overstates its area, so a fill can fail on paper that would pass in the raceway; figuring a standard conductor from Table 5A understates it, and that direction is the violation. The conductor's marking and its manufacturer tell you which stranding you hold.
sections.on_the_job: A 4/0 aluminum compact feeder: open Table 5A, not Table 5, before you tell the foreman the conduit size. The difference between the two tables is regularly the difference between the conduit on the truck and the next size up.
sections.figure_idea: Cross-sections: concentric vs compact stranding at the same AWG, diameters compared.
A four-step flow strip: list conductors, add Table 5 areas, pick Table 1 percent, compare in Table 4.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example, Sharma commercial: three 20 A branch circuits share one EMT — six 12 AWG THHN plus one 12 AWG THHN equipment ground. Seven conductors at 0.0133 sq in each total 0.0931 sq in. Seven conductors take the 40 percent column, and 1/2 in EMT allows 0.122 sq in at 40 percent, so it fits. If the lead picks CCA, one AWG larger under S-10, the same run is seven 10 AWG at 0.0211 — 0.1477 sq in, over 0.122 — and the raceway goes to 3/4 in EMT at 0.213. Say the steps out loud on a mixed pull before you order material. Most failed fills come from a skipped step — a ground left out of the list, an EMT row used for a PVC run, or the 40 percent column used for a two-conductor pull that only gets 31 percent.
sections.plain_explanation:
Every fill problem is the same four steps:
• Step 1 — List every conductor in the raceway, including equipment grounds, with its size and insulation type.
• Step 2 — Take each conductor's area from Table 5 (the Table 8 area for a bare conductor) and add them.
• Step 3 — Pick the Table 1 percentage from the conductor count: 53 for one conductor, 31 for two, 40 for three or more, and 60 for a nipple 24 in or less.
• Step 4 — Open Table 4 for your raceway type and take the first trade size whose usable area at that percentage is equal to or larger than your conductor total. If the total is even slightly over, go up a trade size; close does not count.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 and S-10 apply only when an example uses Sharma's sizing: commercial branch circuits are 20A minimum on 12 AWG copper, and CCA, when the lead picks it, goes one AWG size larger. That is Sharma practice, not a Chapter 9 requirement — the fill method is identical either way, you just take the larger conductor's Table 5 area.

sections.why_it_exists: Conductors need room. In an overfilled raceway the pull jams, insulation scrapes and stretches, and a conductor can be damaged before it ever carries a load. The percentages sit well under the raceway's full area because round conductors do not pack like water — the air between them is part of the math, and two conductors side by side waste the most space, which is why two get the lowest share, 31 percent. Four steps, done in order, make the answer come from the tables instead of from how the pull feels.
inspection_fails: Equipment ground left off the fill list; the pull jams mid-run and insulation comes back scraped.
EMT row of Table 4 used for a PVC run — same trade size name, smaller inside area.
40 percent column used for a two-conductor pull that Table 1 limits to 31 percent.
Conductor total a hair over the Table 4 allowance and the crew pulled it anyway — close does not count.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the two-conductor percentage. Three or more conductors get 40 percent, so 40 feels like the default — but two conductors get only 31 percent, the lowest number in Table 1. The second trap on this page: leaving the equipment ground off the list because 'it carries no current.' Fill does not care what a conductor carries. If it is in the raceway, its area is in the total.

sections.figure_idea: The 0.122 / 0.0133 division worked on a job card, with 9.17 crossed to 9 full conductors and the leftover shown as scrap space.
sections.on_the_job: Default to rounding down. Use the 0.8 round-up only when every conductor in the raceway is truly the same size and type, and be ready to show the inspector the division. Mixed sizes never get the round-up — add their areas instead.
sections.plain_explanation: When every conductor is the same size and type, the count is one division: the raceway's usable area divided by one conductor's area. Worked example from v1: how many 12 AWG THHN fit in 1/2 in EMT? The 40 percent area is 0.122 sq in and one 12 AWG THHN is 0.0133 sq in, so 0.122 / 0.0133 = 9.17 — the answer is 9, because a tenth of a conductor does not exist. One exception, from the Chapter 9 notes carried in v1: when all conductors are the same size and the division leaves a decimal of 0.8 or more, the count may be rounded up to the next whole conductor — 8 AWG THHN in 3/4 in EMT is 0.213 / 0.0366 = 5.82, so 6 are permitted by that note.
sections.title: Same-size fill — divide, then round down

sections.figure_idea: Two stacked bar charts: conductor areas adding to 0.1225 against the 1/2 and 3/4 in EMT limits.
sections.on_the_job: Write each conductor's area on the takeoff, not just the sum. When a run fails by a hair — like the 0.1225 example, over by five ten-thousandths — the written list is how you prove the next trade size was required and not a guess. It is also how the next electrician, adding a circuit to that raceway next year, knows exactly how much room is left: in the 3/4 in EMT from example one, 0.213 - 0.1225 = 0.0905 sq in of the 40 percent allowance is still open.
sections.plain_explanation:
Mixed sizes cannot be divided; each conductor contributes its own Table 5 area and the total is compared with the Table 4 area for the raceway, at the Table 1 percentage for the count.
• Worked example one: two 6 AWG THHN plus one 10 AWG THHN total 2 x 0.0507 + 0.0211 = 0.1225 sq in — just over the 0.122 sq in that 1/2 in EMT allows at 40 percent, so the run goes to 3/4 in EMT at 0.213.
• Worked example two: three 1/0 THHN plus a 6 AWG THHN ground total 3 x 0.1855 + 0.0507 = 0.6072 sq in; 1-1/4 in EMT allows 0.598 and is too small, so 1-1/2 in EMT at 0.814 is the answer.
There is no rounding a mixed total down to fit. Over is over, even by 0.0005 sq in.
sections.title: Mixed-size fill — add the areas
sections.why_it_exists: A mixed pull is where the same-size shortcuts break. One large conductor eats area that a division method assumes is shared evenly, and a total that lands a hair over the limit does not pull like one that lands a hair under — it jams at the bend and skins insulation. Adding the areas one conductor at a time is slower, and it is the only arithmetic that matches what is physically in the pipe.
inspection_fails: Mixed-size pull figured by dividing the raceway area by the largest conductor's area — the smaller conductors' real areas never entered the calculation.
Conductor total rounded down to the raceway allowance on the fill schedule — 0.1225 shown as 0.122.
Ground left off the mixed list; the total passes without it and fails with it.
Annex C count used for a mixed-size pull.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer rounds: '0.1225 is basically 0.122 — it fits.' Fill has no 'basically.' The only round-up in Chapter 9 belongs to same-size division that leaves a remainder of 0.8 or more, and it never applies to a mixed-size total. 0.1225 sq in of conductor in a 0.122 sq in allowance is an overfilled raceway.

sections.figure_idea: A conductor list with the ground line highlighted, showing an insulated ground routed to Table 5 and a bare ground routed to Table 8.
sections.on_the_job: On every fill list, write the ground as its own line with its own area before you add. A Florida home run in 1/2 in EMT: three 12 AWG THHN circuit conductors at 0.0133 sq in each total 0.0399 sq in. With an insulated 12 AWG THHN ground the list totals 0.0532 sq in; with a bare 12 AWG ground it totals 0.0450 sq in. Both fit the 0.122 sq in that 1/2 in EMT allows at 40 percent — but on a tight pull the ground's line is the difference between passing and going up a trade size. Say on the list whether the ground is bare or insulated, and take its area from the right table.
sections.plain_explanation:
An equipment grounding conductor takes up room in the raceway like any other conductor, so it counts in fill — a note to Table 1 says so directly, and says to use the conductor's actual dimensions.
• Insulated ground: take its area from Table 5, in the column for its insulation type. A 12 AWG THHN ground is 0.0133 sq in, the same as any 12 AWG THHN.
• Bare ground: there is no insulation to measure, so Table 5 has no row for it. Take its diameter from Table 8 and use the area of that circle — a bare 12 AWG is 0.081 in across, about 0.0051 sq in.
• One ground, counted once: a shared equipment ground serving several circuits in one raceway still gets its one line on the list.
Leaving the ground out is the most common reason a fill calculation passes on paper and jams in the field.

sections.title: Grounds count, and bare conductors use Table 8
sections.why_it_exists: Fill is physical, not electrical. The ground carries no load current, but the pull does not care — every conductor in the pipe adds friction on the bends and one more chance to skin insulation. A calculation that leaves the ground out approves a raceway the wire cannot actually get through, and the crew finds out halfway through the pull, with the insulation paying for it.
inspection_fails: Fill calculation on the permit set omits the equipment grounding conductor — the raceway is over its Table 1 percentage once the ground is counted.
Bare ground figured at the insulated Table 5 area, or an insulated ground figured as bare — wrong table for the conductor as installed.
Pull jammed mid-run and insulation damaged on a raceway that only passed because the ground was left off the list.
Fill schedule shows no ground line at all for a raceway that contains one.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'The ground does not count — it carries no current.' That mixes up two different checks. Current-carrying status matters for the ampacity adjustment in 310.15(C)(1); fill is about space, and the ground takes space. Count it, at its real area: Table 5 if it is insulated, Table 8 if it is bare.

sections.plain_explanation:
Informative Annex B is the Code's application information for calculating conductor ampacity under engineering supervision — the formula route that accounts for load diversity, conductor arrangement, duct banks and ambient conditions instead of reading a single table cell. Its own tables give ampacities for specific free-air and underground electrical duct arrangements that Table 310.16 does not cover. Two limits define it:
• It is informative, not mandatory. No annex number is a requirement an inspector can cite the way a Chapter 3 section can be cited.
• It is engineering work. The calculation has to be performed and documented for the actual installation by a qualified person — never estimated in the field.
Field sizing stays on the adopted tables: Table 310.16, with the correction and adjustment factors of 310.15. An Annex B number belongs to the design that produced it, with that design's duct spacing, soil conditions and loading assumptions attached.

sections.on_the_job: For a voltage-drop check you need three things off this table and the job: the right metal column, the right stranding row, and resistance in ohm per thousand feet — the formula divides by 1000 because the table is priced per thousand feet, not per foot.
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 8 describes the conductor itself: area in circular mils, stranding, overall diameter, and direct-current resistance at 75 degrees C in ohms per thousand feet, for copper and for aluminum. In the v1 data, stranded copper runs 3.14 ohm/kft at 14 AWG, 1.98 at 12 AWG, 1.24 at 10 AWG, 0.778 at 8 AWG, and 0.491 at 6 AWG — each step up in size drops resistance sharply, which is exactly why upsizing cures voltage drop. Solid and stranded versions of the same AWG have slightly different resistance, so read the row that matches the conductor in hand.

Stranded uncoated copper, DC resistance at 75°C in ohms per 1000 ft — the full run of common sizes, so a voltage-drop check never has to stop at 6 AWG:

• 12 AWG stranded copper — 1.98 Ω/kft
• 10 AWG stranded copper — 1.24 Ω/kft
• 8 AWG stranded copper — 0.778 Ω/kft
• 6 AWG stranded copper — 0.491 Ω/kft
• 4 AWG stranded copper — 0.308 Ω/kft
• 3 AWG stranded copper — 0.245 Ω/kft
• 2 AWG stranded copper — 0.194 Ω/kft
• 1 AWG stranded copper — 0.154 Ω/kft
• 1/0 AWG stranded copper — 0.122 Ω/kft
• 2/0 AWG stranded copper — 0.0967 Ω/kft

flags: CCA is not listed in Table 8 and this book publishes no CCA resistance; a CCA voltage-drop figure requires cited manufacturer data for the actual product at 75 degrees C. v1 README item 7 — carried, not resolved.
sections.on_the_job: If a CCA run needs a voltage-drop answer, do not borrow the aluminum column and report the result as the CCA drop — the aluminum number belongs to aluminum. Get the maker's DC resistance for the actual cable at 75 degrees C, write the source on the calculation, and only then run the formula. If that number is not on hand, the honest status is 'not yet calculated,' and that is what goes on the takeoff.
sections.plain_explanation: Copper-clad aluminum is not in Table 8. The printed table carries copper — uncoated and coated — and aluminum, and nothing else: no CCA column, no CCA row, and this book does not invent one. Ampacity is a different question — there, Table 310.16 reads CCA in its aluminum and copper-clad aluminum column, and S-10 sizes CCA one AWG larger. Voltage drop is where the gap bites, because the resistance has to describe the actual conductor. The aluminum column describes aluminum — 12 AWG stranded aluminum is 3.25 ohm/kft at 75 degrees C — and it is not a CCA value: a drop computed from it must never be reported as a CCA conductor's drop. A CCA resistance has to come from the cable maker's data for the actual product at the operating temperature. Until a cited manufacturer value for the CCA product Sharma installs is on file, this book publishes no CCA voltage-drop figure — the same open point carried on C3-310.16-CCA.

sections.figure_idea: A circuit drawn as a loop — source, out conductor, load, return conductor — with each formula letter pinned to the part it measures.
sections.on_the_job: Use the real load current, not the breaker size, unless the load truly is the breaker size. A 20A circuit carrying a 12A load drops voltage as a 12A circuit, and using 20A will send you upsizing wire the job does not need. Worked check on a Florida house: a 120V workshop receptacle run, 100 ft one-way, actually loaded at 12A, on 12 AWG copper (R = 1.98). VD = 2 x 100 x 1.98 x 12 / 1000 = 4.75V, which is 3.96 percent of 120V — over the 3 percent branch-circuit recommendation. On 10 AWG (R = 1.24) the same run drops 2.98V, 2.48 percent, and passes. The wire changed; nothing else did.
sections.plain_explanation:
Voltage drop is the voltage used up pushing current through the conductor's resistance, out and back. For a single-phase circuit the approximation used here is:
VD = 2 x L x R x I / 1000
• 2 — the round trip. Current travels the length twice, out on one conductor and back on the other. It is the most-forgotten factor in the whole calculation.
• L — the one-way length in feet, as the run is actually routed.
• R — the conductor's resistance from Table 8, in ohms per thousand feet. Stranded copper: 12 AWG is 1.98, 10 AWG is 1.24, 8 AWG is 0.778.
• I — the actual load current in amps, not the breaker size.
• / 1000 — Table 8 is priced per thousand feet, so the division puts the answer in volts.
Finish by turning volts into a percentage: VD divided by the system voltage, times 100. Percent is what the 3 percent and 5 percent recommendations are measured against.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 example sizing only: on a commercial job the starting conductor is 12 AWG copper minimum because Sharma requires 20A branch circuits — if the voltage-drop check then fails, upsize from there. The Code does not impose Sharma's 20A minimum.
sections.title: Voltage drop — the single-phase method
sections.why_it_exists: Voltage lost in the wire is voltage the load never sees. Motors start hard and run hot on low voltage, lights dim, electronics complain — and the lost energy heats the conductor run instead of doing work at the load. The drop grows with length, current and resistance, which is why a circuit that is fine at 30 ft can be a problem at 130 ft on the same breaker.
inspection_fails: Voltage-drop calculation submitted without the round-trip factor — the approved set shows half the drop the run will actually have.
Resistance taken from the aluminum column of Table 8 for a copper run.
Drop reported in volts and compared straight to the 3 percent recommendation, without converting to a percentage of system voltage.
Drop figured at the breaker rating for a load drawing half that, with the wire upsized two sizes past what the load needs.
sections.exam_trap: The classic trap drops the 2: VD = L x R x I / 1000. That figures only the trip out and reports half the real drop — a run that truly drops 6.34V 'passes' at 3.17V on paper. If a voltage-drop answer looks too good for a long run, check for the missing round trip first.

sections.why_it_exists: Every foot of conductor is a small resistance in series with the load, and the current crosses it twice — out and back. Drop grows with length and with current, so a run that serves a load fine at 20 ft can starve the same load at 100 ft. The missing volts never reach the load: lights run dim, and a motor draws more current to make the same power and runs hotter doing it. Working the formula one size at a time is how you land on the smallest conductor that actually serves the load — no guessing, no wasted copper.

sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering with the breaker: 'it is a 20 A circuit, so 12 AWG is fine.' That mixes up two different checks. Ampacity says the conductor will not overheat; voltage drop says the load still gets its voltage at the end of the run. On this page's run, 12 AWG passes ampacity and fails the job at 5.28 percent. The second trap is guessing the jump — going two sizes up 'to be safe' without rerunning the formula, when one variable changed and the same math gives the answer.

sections.on_the_job: Small commercial tenant job: a 208V three-phase load drawing 40A sits 150 ft from the panel, and the 6 AWG copper approximation gives 5.10V — about 2.45 percent, inside the 3 percent recommendation, so no upsize. Label any three-phase result from Table 8 as an approximation when you write it on a takeoff or submittal. If the result lands close to the limit, or the conductors are large, say so and flag it for a Table 9 check by Mike instead of presenting the approximation as exact.
sections.plain_explanation:
For a balanced three-phase circuit, the round-trip factor of 2 is replaced by 1.732, the square root of 3: VD = 1.732 x L x R x I / 1000.
• L is still the one-way length in feet.
• R is still the Table 8 resistance, in ohms per thousand feet.
• I is the load current.
Stated plainly, this is an approximation — it borrows DC resistance from Table 8 for an AC system, and larger conductors, steel raceways, and power factor can move the real answer, which is the work Table 9 exists for. Worked approximation: 40A at 150 ft on 6 AWG copper, 208V three-phase: 1.732 x 150 x 0.491 x 40 / 1000 = 5.10V, about 2.45 percent.

sections.why_it_exists: Three-phase power rides on three conductors sharing the load, so the drop works out to the square root of 3 times the one-way drop instead of twice it. Using the single-phase factor of 2 overstates the drop by about 15 percent and can push an upsize nobody needed. Treating the shortcut as exact runs the other way: on large conductors the real AC impedance moves away from the Table 8 resistance, and a feeder can come up short. The 1.732 method exists for a fast, honest estimate; Table 9 exists for the exact answer.

The mirror-image trap is worse: quoting the 1.732 result as exact on large conductors in steel conduit, where AC resistance and reactance move the real number. sections.florida_note: Florida DOES turn one of them into a mandate for commercial work — through the energy code, not the NEC: FBC Energy Conservation §C405.5.3 requires conductors for feeders and branch circuits in commercial buildings to be sized for a maximum of 5% voltage drop COMBINED. The NEC's own 3%/5% figures remain recommendations; on a Florida commercial job the 5% total is enforceable. Residential work and project specifications are separate questions — check the job documents and the AHJ.
sections.on_the_job: Never tell a customer, a builder, or an inspector that 'the Code requires 3 percent.' Say it the true way: the Code recommends it in an informational note, Sharma designs to it because it keeps equipment happy, and the AHJ and the printed NEC govern. Keep that label on every voltage-drop answer, quiz, and estimate note you write. One exception to keep straight: on a Florida commercial job the combined 5 percent is enforceable through the energy code (see the Florida note) — there the number is a requirement, just not an NEC one.
sections.plain_explanation:
The familiar figures — size a branch circuit so its voltage drop stays near 3 percent, and a feeder plus the branch circuit it supplies near 5 percent total — come from Informational Notes to 210.19(A) and 215.2(A). Informational Notes are guidance, not enforceable requirements, and v1 labels these figures exactly that way.
• Branch circuit: about 3 percent.
• Feeder plus the branch circuit it supplies: about 5 percent total.
• Both figures are recommendations where the NEC states them. Florida commercial work is the exception — see the Florida note.
A circuit over 3 percent is not automatically a code violation; it is a circuit that may run its load poorly — dim lights, a motor that starts hard, equipment that complains — and that a good installer fixes by upsizing, shortening the run, or moving the load.

The notes exist to give designers a target that keeps equipment working the way its nameplate expects — reasonable operating efficiency and performance — without turning a design judgment into a citation. sections.on_the_job:
If a voltage-drop answer matters enough to fight over — a long feeder, a big motor, a plan review comment — do not settle it with the Table 8 approximation. Flag it for Mike to run with Table 9 and the actual raceway and power factor.

Worked example with the effective-Z column: a 208 V three-phase feeder carrying 100 A at 0.85 power factor, 200 ft one-way, on 2 AWG copper in PVC (Z = 0.19 ohm/kft). VD = 1.732 × 200 × 0.19 × 100 / 1000 = 6.58 V, about 3.2 percent of 208 V — over the 3 percent recommendation on the feeder alone, so the design conversation starts at 1 AWG or 1/0, not at hope.
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 9 is the next step past Table 8 for voltage drop. Its full title is 'Alternating-Current Resistance and Reactance for 600-Volt Cables, 3-Phase, 60 Hz, 75 degrees C — Three Single Conductors in Conduit,' and instead of DC resistance alone it gives, in ohms to neutral per 1000 ft, the inductive reactance for all wires, the alternating-current resistance for uncoated copper and for aluminum, and the effective impedance Z at 0.85 power factor — each broken out for PVC, aluminum, and steel conduit, because a magnetic steel raceway raises reactance and, in the larger sizes, AC resistance as well. The table's Note 1 limits its values to conductors at 75 degrees C under the conditions its title states. the teaching here is when to reach for it — large conductors, long three-phase runs, steel raceway, or a Table 8 approximation that lands near a limit — and to run those cases from the printed table rather than from memory. Common copper sizes are carried below (aluminum and sizes above 4/0 stay in the printed table) — uncoated copper, ohms to neutral per 1000 ft. Reactance and the effective-Z column are the parts Table 8 cannot give you; the AC resistance column tracks Table 8 closely at small sizes and climbs above it in steel conduit as sizes grow. Sizes above 4/0, and the aluminum columns, stay in the printed table:

Tables 11(A) and 11(B) — how much power a Class 2 or Class 3 source may deliver
sections.plain_explanation: Tables 11(A) and 11(B) are the numbers behind the words 'power limited.' For Class 2 and Class 3 circuits, the tables cap what the power source may deliver — maximum circuit voltage, maximum current, and maximum volt-amperes — with one table for ac sources and one for dc sources. Each table splits sources two ways: inherently limited sources, whose construction keeps them inside the limits under any load or fault, and sources that are not inherently limited and therefore rely on overcurrent protection sized from the table. Article 725 sends you here to decide whether a transformer or supply really is a Class 2 source; a 'Class 2' claim on a nameplate is checked against these tables, not taken on faith.
sections.on_the_job: A door-control transformer marked Class 2: the table row for its voltage is what makes that marking true, and it is also what earns the wiring-method freedoms Chapter 7 gives Class 2 circuits. No table match, no Class 2 treatment — the circuit is wired like power.

sections.florida_note: Annex D is informative. The mandatory calculation rules are the Chapter 2 articles as adopted in Florida; the annex only illustrates them.
sections.on_the_job: When a load calc is due, work it in the annex's order — general loads, then the named appliances and motors, then demand, then the service size — and keep the arithmetic with the estimate so Mike can re-run it. If your total and the annex pattern disagree, the inputs are wrong somewhere, not the pattern.
sections.plain_explanation: Annex D shows the load-calculation articles worked end to end on example buildings: add the loads the articles name, apply the demand factors the articles allow, and arrive at a service or feeder size. The 2020 annex works eight example families: D1, a one-family dwelling by the standard method, with and without air conditioning; D2, a one-family dwelling by the optional method of 220.82, including a heat-pump version with backup heat; D3, a store building; D4 and D5, multifamily dwellings — D5 served at 208Y/120 volts, three-phase; D6, maximum demand for range loads from Table 220.55; D7, dwelling service conductors sized with 310.12; and D8, motor conductors and protection under Article 430. This book teaches that method and points you to the real work in Chapter 2 — especially the optional dwelling calculation data carried in v1 as table 220.82 — rather than copying an annex example. A Sharma example must be computed fresh from the actual house, labeled as a Sharma example, and checked; an annex example is a pattern to follow, not a number to borrow for a different building.

sections.on_the_job: Reach for the equipment marking first, the manufacturer instruction second, and a general recommended table only when neither exists — and use a torque tool, not a guess by feel, on service and feeder lugs.
sections.plain_explanation: Informative Annex I is titled 'Recommended Tightening Torque Tables from UL Standard 486A-B,' and it collects recommended tightening-torque values for connections in three tables: Table I.1, for screws No. 10 and larger, including split-bolt and other connectors; Table I.2, for slotted head screws smaller than No. 10, intended for use with conductors 8 AWG and smaller; and Table I.3, for screws with recessed Allen or square drives. It is a fallback, not the first stop: 110.14(D) makes the manufacturer's stated torque the rule, achieved by an approved means, and the annex tables serve the connection where the equipment gives no torque value and none can be obtained from the manufacturer. This page publishes no torque values — torque comes off the equipment marking, the manufacturer's instructions, or the annex tables in the printed book, never from memory.

sections.on_the_job: When someone quotes an annex at you on a job, ask the deciding question: is that in a mandatory section, or in an annex or a note? Both can be good practice; only one can be enforced as written, and knowing which keeps you from arguing the wrong point with an inspector.
sections.plain_explanation:
The annexes sit behind the mandatory chapters as explanation, examples, and reference data. Unless an adopting ordinance specifically adopts an annex, its content is not a requirement an inspector can cite the way a numbered article section can be cited — that is the same status the 3 and 5 percent voltage-drop figures carry as Informational Notes. This chapter covers the annexes Sharma work actually touches — C for same-size fill checks, D for calculation examples, and I for torque. The remaining annex letters were not written as pages in this pass, because their letters and subjects were not confirmed against the printed 2020 book, and this book does not invent an annex.

Update since this page was first written: Annex B has since been added as a brief page (C9-ANNEXB), scoped the same way as the annexes above — what it is, when it is used, and no reproduced ampacity tables. Table 5A, Tables 11(A)/(B) and Annex B now have their own pages. Still held back: Table 10 (stranding), Table 12 (PLFA power source limits), and the annex letters not yet written. The 2020 informative annexes are A (product safety standards), B (ampacity calculation), C (same-size fill tables), D (examples), E (types of construction), F (critical operations power systems), G (SCADA), H (administration and enforcement), I (torque tables from UL 486A-B) and J (ADA standards). Annex K is new in NEC 2023, so the 2020 book has none.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• Annex K: New Informative Annex K, Use of Medical Electrical Equipment in Dwellings and Residential Board-and-Care Occupancies. (So the 2020 book correctly has no Annex K.)
